summary:
Washington stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry screening, which applies in every state. An executive order of 20 January 2025 redefined sex for national purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the national justice department to "correct the misapplication" of a 2020 Supreme Court employment ruling. The national foreign-affairs department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, while X-marker passports issued before the change remain valid until expiry. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a departmental policy in place since 1992; the policy remains challenged in the federal courts, and trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports confiscated or blocked at processing by March 2025, some stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries its own exposure nationwide. Following an executive order of 5 February 2025 on women's sports, the foreign-affairs department announced on 25 February 2025 that it would bar trans athletes from entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. Transport-security checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Against that national backdrop, a July 2026 legal risk assessment names Washington among the most protective states in the country. The same assessment groups Washington with Colorado, Hawaii and Maryland as states holding comprehensive health-insurance laws that cover facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures, and records refugee protections for people fleeing hostile states.

Two ballot initiatives scheduled for November, I-001 and I-638, are flagged by that assessment as targeting transgender residents. They are proposals rather than enacted law at the time of assessment, and the sources do not record a result.

Custody in Washington has produced documented harm. In October 2023 Washington state prisons were legally required, under court order and rulings, to provide gender-affirming healthcare and/or sexual-reassignment surgery to inmates. In July 2024 a trans woman prisoner was transferred from a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison, so birth-sex housing was used as a sanction.
tangentialFactors:
Washington's protective standing is comparative rather than absolute. The July 2026 assessment places it in the same tier as Colorado, Hawaii and Maryland on health-insurance coverage for gender-affirming procedures, and lists it among states covered by a nationwide tracker of shield measures against out-of-state action. Coverage in neighbouring or peer states does not travel with the visitor: the insurance obligations attach to Washington-resident policies.

The two November initiatives are the main source of turbulence identified in the inventory. They are assessed as targeting transgender residents, but the sources give no text, sponsorship detail or outcome, so the direction of any change they would make is unresolved.

National measures in force or in litigation elsewhere in the country, including the military purge, the women's sports ban, a January 2025 funding freeze and October 2025 rules affecting care funding, have been blocked or enjoined in part in the courts, so the operative position on any given federal measure should be checked before travel.
localsOnly:
Washington maintains shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches that are enforceable against out-of-state action, and the state is listed among those covered by a nationwide tracker of such measures. For residents this is the machinery that limits cooperation with, and reach of, hostile-state orders targeting gender-affirming care.

Health-insurance coverage for gender-affirming procedures is comparatively broad: the laws cover facial hair removal and an expanded range of procedures, placing Washington alongside Colorado, Hawaii and Maryland. The assessment also records refugee protections for people who move to Washington to escape restrictive laws in other states.

The custody findings are resident-facing. A 2023 court order obliged Washington prisons to provide gender-affirming healthcare and/or sexual-reassignment surgery to inmates; the July 2024 transfer shows that birth-sex housing can nonetheless be imposed as discipline, and no later reporting on that practice is in the inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not state whether initiatives I-001 and I-638 reached the ballot, were adopted, or were blocked; no text or sponsorship is sourced.

Unresolved: the inventory carries no reporting after July 2024 on Washington prison housing practice, and no figures on how many trans inmates are held in the state system.

Not sourced: Washington's own rules for changing a gender marker on a state driver's licence or birth certificate, and whether any 2026 state-level document invalidation measures apply in Washington. Visitors should verify the state document position separately from the federal passport position.

Unresolved: the operative status of the federal passport and visa measures at the time of travel, since the challenges cited remain in the federal courts and several related executive orders have been enjoined in part.
